tweets.title:
Train on what you know, let the biology emerge in the representation

Scientific labels are often noisy or incomplete. Sometimes the better strategy is not to t
tweets.body:
Train on what you know, let the biology emerge in the representation

Scientific labels are often noisy or incomplete. Sometimes the better strategy is not to train the model on the biological concept you ultimately want to discover.

Krentzel and coauthors train an EfficientNet-B0 on a much cleaner task: given a brightfield image of bacteria, predict which antibiotic and concentration produced it.

The network is never explicitly trained to recognize how the drug works. Yet antibiotics with the same mechanism naturally end up close together in the learned feature space. The representation captures biological similarity even though the supervision contains only experimental-condition labels.

That becomes useful for compounds the model has never seen. A simple nearest-neighbour search in this feature space assigns unseen antibiotics to known mechanisms, and even predicted that relebactam targets PBP2, a result the authors then confirmed experimentally with an independent binding assay.

When the scientific label is uncertain, train on the experimental facts you know reliably and ask whether the biology organizes itself in the learned representation.

Krentzel et al., Nature Communications (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/vdW9sPgBzh

tweets.title:
Better AI-for-science should mean smarter use of the same budget

A fair AI benchmark should ask whether the model can use the same resources more intelligently
tweets.body:
Better AI-for-science should mean smarter use of the same budget

A fair AI benchmark should ask whether the model can use the same resources more intelligently, not whether it can win by using more.

That is exactly what Zimmer and coauthors do for glioblastoma radiotherapy. A model could trivially cover more of a future tumor recurrence by treating a larger region of the brain, so they forbid that. Every AI-generated treatment region must have exactly the same volume as the standard plan.

The U-Net predicts where the tumor is most likely to return and redistributes that fixed treatment volume toward those higher-risk areas.

With no extra treatment volume, coverage of future recurrence increases from 77.34% to 79.37%, with gains of at least 5 percentage points in 19.3% of patients.

The idea is much broader than medicine: whether the scarce resource is experiments, simulation calls, measurements, energy, or treatment volume, compare AI systems at the same budget. Otherwise, “better” may simply mean “more.”

Zimmer et al., npj Digital Medicine (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/LACWCn6hFw

tweets.title:
Bayesian optimization turns a trusted physics simulator into an autonomous surface-structure solver

For electron diffraction, predicting the spectrum from a kn
tweets.body:
Bayesian optimization turns a trusted physics simulator into an autonomous surface-structure solver

For electron diffraction, predicting the spectrum from a known surface is already possible. The difficult part is running that physics backward: finding the atomic structure that produced the measured spectrum.

Tang and coauthors do not train a neural network to learn that inverse map. They keep the full multiple-scattering simulator inside the loop and use Bayesian optimization to decide which candidate structure should be simulated next.

The clever part is the division of labor: physics evaluates each candidate; ML decides where to search. Crystallographic symmetry reduces the search space, while adaptive trust regions move between broad exploration and local refinement.

That also lets quantities normally tuned in separate manual steps (atomic positions, thermal vibrations, even experimental beam alignment) be optimized together.

For the more complex Fe₂O₃ surface, the method handles a 53-variable inverse problem in a single automated loop, recovering a physically consistent structure and experimental incidence angle without the usual manually defined refinement hierarchy.

If the forward physics is trustworthy but inversion is expensive, don’t necessarily learn the inverse model. Keep the simulator and learn how to search it efficiently.

Tang et al., npj Computational Materials (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/912kl91BKb

tweets.title:
In science, model capacity is only useful if your data can support it

Data scarcity is common in scientific problems. In that regime, increasing complexity oft
tweets.body:
In science, model capacity is only useful if your data can support it

Data scarcity is common in scientific problems. In that regime, increasing complexity often buys you variance before it buys you performance.

A classical ML model or a shallow network may reach its useful regime quickly, while a deeper model can require much more data before its extra capacity becomes an advantage.

So the relevant question is not:

“Which model is more powerful?”

It is:

“Do I have enough data to exploit that power?”

A practical way to check is with a learning curve: train on progressively larger fractions of the dataset and track validation performance. If the curve has already saturated, more capacity may not help. If performance is still climbing strongly, a more expressive model may have room to win.

In experimental science, model selection is partly a question of where you are on the data axis.

This is one of the ideas I discuss in my textbook Inteligencia artificial para estudiantes de ciencias (Ediciones Pirámide).

tweets.title:
The right pretraining data lets a 110M DNA model rival a 7B model at finding hidden viral DNA

Bigger is not always better if the model has learned from the wro
tweets.body:
The right pretraining data lets a 110M DNA model rival a 7B model at finding hidden viral DNA

Bigger is not always better if the model has learned from the wrong biology.

Finding prophages means locating viral DNA embedded inside bacterial genomes. Lindsey and coauthors use this as a stress test for genomic language models trained on very different kinds of DNA.

The striking comparison is ProkBERT-mini-long, a BERT-style model pretrained specifically on prokaryotic DNA, against EVO2, a 7-billion-parameter genomic model trained across many species.

ProkBERT-mini-long is roughly 60× smaller, yet its genome-wide detection performance is almost the same: 0.700 versus 0.719.

The useful lesson goes well beyond genomics: before scaling a scientific foundation model, ask whether its pretraining data actually contain the world you want it to understand. Better domain alignment can buy more than billions of extra parameters.

Lindsey et al., NAR Genomics and Bioinformatics (2026), https://t.co/6no6lI3y9Y

tweets.title:
Physical feature learning in a random laser enables few-shot vision

A random laser doesn’t need to be trained to become a neural network. Its physics already d
tweets.body:
Physical feature learning in a random laser enables few-shot vision

A random laser doesn’t need to be trained to become a neural network. Its physics already does much of the feature extraction.

In the 150-μm InP network, many lasing modes overlap and compete for the same optical gain. Some modes are activated while others are suppressed, creating excitatory and inhibitory nonlinear responses that make different modes sensitive to different image features in parallel.

Ng and coauthors then keep that physical network fixed and train only a simple linear readout on the resulting hyperspectral responses. The useful representation comes from the device’s disorder, mode competition, and heterogeneous nonlinearities, not from backpropagating through millions of weights.

On the BreakHis breast-cancer histology task, the system reaches 77.7% accuracy from just 10 training images, and outperforms their pretrained vision-transformer benchmark up to 200 training images.

When the physics already gives you a useful representation, train around it, not through it.

Ng et al., Science Advances (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/meHI2Ey3Ah

tweets.title:
The most useful machine-learning model in a scientific lab is often not a neural network.

A biologist with 50 patient samples, a chemist with 100 synthesized c
tweets.body:
The most useful machine-learning model in a scientific lab is often not a neural network.

A biologist with 50 patient samples, a chemist with 100 synthesized compounds, or a physicist with a few hundred expensive measurements is working in a very different regime from the datasets that made deep learning famous.

In that regime, regularized regression, random forests, SVMs or Gaussian processes can be the better tools, especially when uncertainty and honest validation matter as much as raw accuracy.

Deep learning is extraordinarily powerful. But sophistication is not the goal. The goal is to use the model that matches the science and the data.

That is one of the first ideas in my new textbook, "Inteligencia artificial para estudiantes de ciencias" (Ediciones Pirámide).

tweets.title:
Teach a graph neural network where a protein starts shouldn’t matter and hidden structural relationships emerge

Two proteins can have essentially the same 3D f
tweets.body:
Teach a graph neural network where a protein starts shouldn’t matter and hidden structural relationships emerge

Two proteins can have essentially the same 3D fold even when their chains start and end at different positions. Yet structure-search models can miss that relationship because their embeddings still encode where the protein chain begins and ends.

Kolodziej and coauthors take a very direct approach with CIRPIN. They train an E(n)-equivariant graph neural network on synthetic circular permutations of protein structures, using supervised contrastive learning so that different reorderings of the same structural topology land close together in embedding space.

The important point is that they do not throw away positional information. They teach the model which changes in that information should not matter.

That is enough to uncover protein relationships hidden from conventional searches, including four distinct topological forms of the PDZ domain related by circular permutation.

For AI for Science: if you already know which transformations should preserve scientific meaning, don’t make the model rediscover that invariance from scratch. Put it into the training process.

Kolodziej et al., PNAS (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/Du8OoxAqnU

tweets.title:
Una distinción mil veces contada.

La IA contiene al aprendizaje automático. El aprendizaje automático contiene al deep learning.

La lectura habitual: lo inter
tweets.body:
Una distinción mil veces contada.

La IA contiene al aprendizaje automático. El aprendizaje automático contiene al deep learning.

La lectura habitual: lo interesante está en el centro.

La realidad en un laboratorio científico: lo interesante a veces está en el anillo de en medio.

Doscientos puntos de un experimento a veces no piden una red profunda. Piden un proceso gaussiano, un bosque aleatorio o una regresión con regularización. Y sobre todo piden barras de error, porque la barra de error es lo que decide qué mides después.

No todo el aprendizaje automático es deep learning. Y en IA para ciencia, lo clásico a veces no es lo antiguo sino lo adecuado.

https://t.co/OHyit1aHnA

tweets.title:
Don’t make ML solve a bad intermediate problem

Many scientific pipelines contain an intermediate step that exists mostly because that is how the field has trad
tweets.body:
Don’t make ML solve a bad intermediate problem

Many scientific pipelines contain an intermediate step that exists mostly because that is how the field has traditionally processed the data.

Here, multiview calcium imaging is usually turned into a reconstructed 3D volume before neurons are extracted. But that reconstruction is itself ill-posed: scattering and noise can create errors before the biological analysis even starts.

Chen and coauthors avoid that step. DeepWonder3D works directly on the multiview projections, using 3D U-Nets for denoising, background removal and neuronal extraction, then combining temporal agreement across views with a physics-based optical model to recover each neuron’s 3D position.

On terabyte-scale cortical recordings, the pipeline extracts thousands of neurons in hours and runs about 10× faster than the reconstruction-based comparison method.

Sometimes the best model improvement is not a better network, but removing an unstable intermediate representation from the workflow.

Chen et al., Nature Methods (2026), journal license, https://t.co/89emL8mO3u

tweets.title:
Synthetic-physics training lets a vision transformer detect weaker methane plumes from space

Training a model to find methane leaks from space runs into a fami
tweets.body:
Synthetic-physics training lets a vision transformer detect weaker methane plumes from space

Training a model to find methane leaks from space runs into a familiar problem for the AI-for-science community: satellite images are abundant, but exact labels for where each plume is, how strong it is, and where it starts are not.

Batchu and coauthors solve this by simulating 3.6 million methane plumes with a physical dispersion model and radiative-transfer calculations, then injecting them into real EMIT satellite observations. The plume is synthetic (and therefore perfectly labeled) but the terrain, atmosphere, surface reflectance, and sensor noise remain real.

MAPL-EMIT then uses a Swin Transformer encoder inside a U-Net-like architecture to combine the full hyperspectral signal with spatial context. From the same input, it predicts methane enhancement, plume boundaries, and source location, even when several plumes overlap.

That training strategy matters. Instead of trying to simulate an entire satellite scene realistically, the authors simulate only the physical phenomenon for which ground truth is missing.

On real observations, the model recovers 84% of NASA’s expert-annotated plume complexes while identifying about 1.5× as many plausible plumes overall, with much of the gain coming from weaker emissions.

The broader lesson is: when ground truth is scarce, simulate the phenomenon you need to learn, but keep the surrounding world real.

Batchu et al., PNAS (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/Fj5jgLkH3B

tweets.title:
Don’t optimize the proxy. Optimize your whole scientific system.

Here, making the enzyme faster does not necessarily make the cell produce more.

The terminal
tweets.body:
Don’t optimize the proxy. Optimize your whole scientific system.

Here, making the enzyme faster does not necessarily make the cell produce more.

The terminal enzyme NeuB consumes phosphoenolpyruvate, a metabolite the cell also needs for growth and central metabolism. Pushing that reaction too hard can therefore hurt the pathway as a whole.

Wang and coauthors use DLCatalysis to rank 6,612 NeuB variants. The model combines ProtT5 protein-sequence embeddings with molecular fingerprints and graph-based substrate representations, then uses bidirectional cross-attention to learn how the enzyme and substrate interact.

Crucially, they do not test only the highest-ranked mutants. They deliberately sample across the predicted activity range.

That reveals the important result: a less active NeuB variant raises NeuAc production from 8.54 to 9.27 g L⁻¹, because it better balances product formation with the cell’s competing metabolic needs.

Use ML to explore the trade-offs of the whole system, not just to maximize a local score.

Wang et al., Nature Communications (2026), CC BY-NC-ND 4.0. https://t.co/y0fxwjUlOo

tweets.title:
A better way to judge foundation models: not only by what they can predict zero-shot, but by how much expensive science they can amortize.

The real test of a s
tweets.body:
A better way to judge foundation models: not only by what they can predict zero-shot, but by how much expensive science they can amortize.

The real test of a scientific foundation model may not be zero-shot accuracy. It may be how little new high-quality data it needs to become trustworthy on a new problem.

Thermal conductivity is a demanding case because it depends on subtle anharmonic atomic interactions, not just getting energies approximately right.

Póta and coauthors use a pretrained atomistic foundation model as the reusable prior, then fine-tune only what is material-specific. The learned potential provides the interatomic forces, while the Wigner transport equation keeps the heat-transport physics explicit. For LiBr, that adaptation requires just 3 new DFT configurations.

With those 3 configurations, the thermal-conductivity error drops from about 47% to 2%.

Póta et al., Nature Communications (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/0U1L0eOXsi

tweets.title:
Generative AI explores protein architectures evolution never tried

Viruses are extraordinarily good at transporting genetic material, yet evolution has repeate
tweets.body:
Generative AI explores protein architectures evolution never tried

Viruses are extraordinarily good at transporting genetic material, yet evolution has repeatedly converged on a relatively narrow family of capsid shapes. That does not mean those shapes are optimal for an RNA delivery vehicle built for the laboratory.

Here, generative protein design is used to step outside that evolutionary search space. RFdiffusion creates synthetic protein assemblies with unusual cyclic and dihedral symmetries. Known biological domains are then retained for membrane binding, budding and RNA capture. AI designs the scaffold, while biology supplies the functions that already work. 

The best design, based on an unusual C8 planar assembly, required more than 10,000× less mRNA than a lipid nanoparticle to produce the same expression level in the reported cellular comparison.

Generative AI can search physically possible biology that evolution never had a reason to explore.

Schuhmacher et al., Nature (2026), CC BY 4.0. https://t.co/eKtoHQCvZt

tweets.title:
AI may matter most when it stops tuning experiments and starts inventing them

With just 10 interferometry components, there can already be more than a billion
tweets.body:
AI may matter most when it stops tuning experiments and starts inventing them

With just 10 interferometry components, there can already be more than a billion possible experimental topologies. Human intuition can explore only a tiny fraction of that space.

One particularly powerful idea is to start with an overcomplete experiment: deliberately include more components than necessary, let optimization continuously change their importance and physical parameters, evaluate every candidate with a physics simulator, and then prune away what is not needed.

The clever part is the division of labour: physics predicts what each experiment would do, AI searches for which experiment should exist.

That changes experimental design from optimizing a known apparatus into searching over the apparatus itself.

AI for Science may become most consequential not by replacing scientific models, but by exploring experimental possibilities that humans would never think to test.

Klimesch et al., Nature (2026), journal license, https://t.co/zFeGTEBYrt

tweets.title:
Hoy es el día: ya está disponible "Inteligencia artificial para estudiantes de ciencias" (Ediciones Pirámide, Grupo Anaya). 📘

Es el libro de IA que me habría g
tweets.body:
Hoy es el día: ya está disponible "Inteligencia artificial para estudiantes de ciencias" (Ediciones Pirámide, Grupo Anaya). 📘

Es el libro de IA que me habría gustado tener cuando empecé a aplicar aprendizaje automático a problemas científicos.

Está pensado para estudiantes e investigadores/as de física, química, biología, matemáticas y otras disciplinas científicas. Por eso, los ejemplos no parten de problemas genéricos de informática, sino de ciencia: espectroscopía, propiedades moleculares, el modelo de Ising o el diseño de materiales para baterías.

El recorrido va desde los fundamentos (generalización, sobreajuste, las matemáticas del aprendizaje) hasta las redes neuronales profundas, los modelos generativos, los transformers y el aprendizaje por refuerzo.

La idea es entender no solo cómo utilizar estas técnicas, sino qué están haciendo, por qué funcionan y cuándo tiene sentido aplicarlas a un problema científico, incluso en el régimen de pocos datos tan habitual en la ciencia experimental.

Y había algo que para mí era especialmente importante: cada capítulo viene acompañado de un notebook disponible en abierto en GitHub, preparado para ejecutarse directamente en Google Colab, sin instalar nada. Los notebooks permiten trabajar de forma práctica los conceptos del capítulo y hacen que el libro pueda utilizarse tanto para el estudio individual como directamente en el aula.

Ya está disponible en las principales librerías y plataformas online:

📘 https://t.co/OHyit1bfd8

———

🇬🇧 Artificial Intelligence for Science Students is out today with Ediciones Pirámide.

A bridge between traditional scientific training and machine learning, from the fundamentals of generalization and regression to deep learning, transformers and reinforcement learning, with examples drawn throughout from real scientific problems.

Written in Spanish, with an open, Colab-ready notebook accompanying every chapter, available on GitHub.

Now available in bookstores and online:

https://t.co/OHyit1bfd8

tweets.title: In terms of the used ML implementation, pySTED employs deep learning architectures, such as U-Net, to generate realistic data maps of biological structures, whi
tweets.body:
In terms of the used ML implementation, pySTED employs deep learning architectures, such as U-Net, to generate realistic data maps of biological structures, which are then used to create synthetic images. These images are used to train convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for tasks like semantic segmentation, enhancing AI model performance in microscopy. 

Additionally, pySTED supports RL training via an OpenAI Gym environment, allowing agents to interact with the simulation to optimize imaging parameters, such as laser power and pixel dwell time. This setup enables RL agents to be trained entirely in simulation, then deployed successfully on real microscopes without the need for fine-tuning, bridging the gap between simulation and reality. (2/2)
